problem: The trap says a change of final drive changes the reading. That is true only when the speed sensor sits at the gearbox output. When the sensor is at the wheels, changing the final drive ratio does not change the pulses per km, so the speedometer reading stays the same. A student can carry away a wrong rule.
fix: It is driven by wheel or gearbox pulses, so a change of tyre size changes the reading in both cases; a change of final drive changes it only when the sensor is on the gearbox output shaft, not when it is at the wheels.

problem: Section 2 defines C as the tyre rolling circumference and N as pulses per wheel revolution, which is correct for a wheel sensor. For a gearbox-output sensor the same formula needs the distance travelled per revolution of that shaft, that is, tyre circumference divided by the final drive ratio. The chapter does not say this, so the formula is applied blindly to both sensor positions. Separately, Q1 answers that the coolant gauge is in °C while it is marked C to H, which contradicts Section 1, where the gauge has no unit and only end marks.
fix: Add one line to Section 2: for a gearbox-output sensor, C is the distance the vehicle moves per revolution of that shaft, equal to the tyre rolling circumference divided by the final drive ratio. In Q1 answer: coolant temperature gauge marked C to H (cold to hot), read as a relative scale with no numeric °C markings on most clusters.

problem: "Its return detent" is unclear. Cluster stepper motors have no return spring; the needle comes back because the driver chip steps the motor back. As written, a student may think a spring or detent brings the needle home.
fix: It is a self-test. A full-scale sweep and return proves the stepper motor, its driver and the gear train work and that the motor can be commanded back to the zero step. A needle that does not move points to a failed motor or driver before the car moves.
